title: 12 Questions to Ask a Commercial Renovation Contractor

metaDescription: Twelve questions to ask before you hire a renovation company for a rental building, office or storefront: experience, permits, money and warranties.

answer: Ask what similar work the contractor has finished, who can vouch for it, whether its WCB clearance and liability insurance are current, who runs the job, and which permits apply. Then ask what the quote includes, how allowances and change orders work, what the payment schedule is, and what warranty applies.

blocks.x: Hiring a renovation company for a rental building, office or storefront is different from hiring one for a home. Tenants are affected, permits are more involved, schedules are tighter, and mistakes cost rent. These 12 questions to ask a commercial contractor before you sign anything help you choose a renovation company that can handle commercial and multi-unit work.
Questions about the renovation company

**1. What similar projects have you completed in the last two years?** Ask how many projects like yours they've finished, such as occupied apartment turns, office fit-outs, restaurants, clinics or retail, and what went wrong on one of them. A specific answer tells you more than a portfolio.
**2. Can you provide references from property managers or business owners?** Call at least two. Ask whether the job finished on time and on budget, and how problems were handled.

**3. Do you have current WCB Manitoba clearance and liability insurance?** The answer matters: WCB Manitoba warns you might be liable for the assessment costs of a firm that isn't in good standing. Check for yourself: pull [a clearance letter](/blog/how-to-check-a-contractors-wcb-clearance-manitoba) from WCB's public Clearance Request System before work starts and again before each payment. Ask for a certificate of insurance.
About the project
**4. Who manages the job day to day?** You want one named project lead who answers your calls.

**5. Will you handle permits and inspections?** Commercial renovations in Winnipeg often need a building permit, plus plumbing, electrical or mechanical permits. A [change of use](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) starts with a building permit application, then an occupancy permit. Make sure the contractor knows the process.
**6. How will you work around tenants or customers?** Ask about work hours, noise, dust control, protecting common areas, and keeping exits and fire systems working.
**7. What's your realistic schedule, including permit time?** Get a start date, a duration and key milestones in writing.
About the money
**8. What exactly is included in the quote?** Look for a detailed scope with materials, finishes and quantities, not a single lump sum.
**9. What's priced as an allowance?** Allowances (for fixtures, flooring, counters) can grow. Know which items are firm and which aren't.
**10. How do change orders work?** Any extra work should be priced and approved in writing before it's done.
**11. What's the payment schedule?** Expect a reasonable deposit and progress payments tied to completed work.

In Manitoba you also keep back 7.5% of each payment, for at least 60 days after the earliest of three events: substantial performance is certified, the work is completed, or it is abandoned. On larger contracts it goes into a holdback account. Our guide to [the builders' lien holdback](/blog/builders-lien-holdback-manitoba) explains how it works.
After the job
**12. What warranty do you provide, and how do I request service?** Get warranty terms in writing, along with how quickly they respond to deficiencies.
Watch for these warning signs
No written contract or a vague one-line scope
Large cash deposits up front
Suggesting you skip permits to save time
No clearance letter or certificate of insurance
Payment instructions that change by email
The bottom line
Get each contractor's answers in writing and compare them side by side. If a contractor dodges these questions, keep looking.
General information, not legal advice. Ask a lawyer how the holdback applies to your contract.
